name: Ñanchoc mixed crop food production
description: Ñanchoc Valley inhabitants consumed cultivated squash and peanuts alongside other plants within a mixed food-production and foraging economy. Later Tierra Blanca evidence points to more intensive cultivation, with fields worked beyond individual household gardens and small irrigation canals in the same valley.

impact.note: One valley's community added cultivated squash and peanuts to foraging; a new way of getting food, with later Andean cultivation following nearby.

date.label: By approximately 8600 cal BP (6650 BCE)
date.basis: Authors infer a diverse farming system by about 8000 radiocarbon years BP, approximately 8600 calibrated BP; this is not a direct date for every crop residue.

events.statement: Ñanchoc Valley inhabitants consumed cultivated squash and peanuts alongside other plants within a mixed food-production and foraging economy.
events.caveats: The authors infer the wider farming system from multiple classes of evidence; starch in teeth is evidence of consumption, not by itself proof of local cultivation or independent domestication of every plant.

evidence.supports: The authors place a diverse food-production system by approximately 8000 radiocarbon years BP, approximately 8600 calibrated years BP.

date.label: Tierra Blanca phase, c. 7800–5000 cal BP (5850–3050 BCE)
date.basis: The 2011 excavation synthesis gives this calibrated phase interval. The interval provides context for a shift in cultivation whose onset and duration remain unresolved.

events.statement: Archaeologists interpret the Tierra Blanca evidence in the Ñanchoc Valley as a shift toward more intensive cultivation, with fields worked by multiple households and small-scale irrigation in the valley.
events.scope: Phase-level transition in Ñanchoc crop production.
events.caveats: The field below the dated canals remains undated, and the crops grown there are unidentified. Directly dated cotton from CA-09-71 came from a house floor.

evidence.locator: Chapter 9, public summary, final paragraph; same volume, chapter 1, dating convention
evidence.supports: The synthesis dates Tierra Blanca to 7800–5000 calibrated BP and describes the shift from single-family gardens to multifamily fields and canal systems in the upper valley.
The study reports plant remains, planting plots, stone hoes and small irrigation canals across Tierra Blanca contexts. The analyzed teeth come from earlier Las Pircas occupations.

evidence.locator: pp. 1890–1891, crop descriptions and Fig. 5; p. 1892, Table 1, CA-09-71
evidence.supports: The paper reports peanut remains and quinoa-like chenopods at Tierra Blanca sites. Cotton recovered from a house floor at CA-09-71 dates to 6278–5948 cal BP.

evidence.locator: pp. 17243–17244, Fig. 3 and discussion of the lower bench and garden sites
evidence.supports: The lower-bench agricultural field contained hoe-like implements and is undated. The probable earlier garden furrows at CA-09-27 and CA-09-52 are on a separate fan.

earliest_record.rationale: Earliest source-supported dated event for this scoped record; not a global priority claim. The authors infer the wider farming system from multiple classes of evidence; starch in teeth is evidence of consumption, not by itself proof of local cultivation or independent domestication of every plant.

caveats: The authors infer the wider farming system from multiple classes of evidence; starch in teeth is evidence of consumption, not by itself proof of local cultivation or independent domestication of every plant.

research.note: The Las Pircas event and other facets marked reviewed were independently checked on 2026-11-09. The Tierra Blanca event and Canal 3 question are sourced proposals.

unresolved.about: Cultivated species on Tierra Blanca plots
unresolved.note: Dated botanical remains from a field horizon or a secure physical link between a field and a canal would clarify crop identities and irrigation practice. The directly dated cotton sample comes from a house floor, and the dental starch evidence comes from earlier Las Pircas contexts.

evidence.supports: The cotton sample was recovered from a buried house floor.
The 39 teeth came from Las Pircas occupations.

measures.subject: Human teeth from Las Pircas occupations at four Ñanchoc Valley sites
measures.conditions: The study examined 39 teeth from four sites, associated with multiple dates from 8210 ± 180 to 6970 ± 60 radiocarbon years BP; this is not an adoption count or a sample all from one date.

evidence.supports: Authors examined 39 human teeth from Las Pircas occupations at four sites.

date.label: By publication in 2008
date.basis: The 2008 study reports the sample size; the teeth come from multiple archaeological contexts.

links.statement: Did cultivation on the buried lower-bench field depend on water delivered by Canal 3?
links.scope: The water-delivery function of Canal 3 and cultivation on the buried lower-bench field at Quebrada sin Nombre-1.
links.timing: The Canal 3 fill age falls within the 2011 Tierra Blanca phase interval. The lower-bench field's age remains open.
links.finding: The excavators proposed a shared destination on the lower bench when comparing the canal gradients and flows. That model is consistent with irrigation there. The field remains undated and an excavated outlet from Canal 3 has not been traced to it.

evidence.locator: pp. 17242–17244, Figs. 1–3 and discussion of the lower bench
evidence.supports: The canals lie above a lower bench identified as a probable field location. The report gives a fill age for Canal 3 and describes the buried field as undated.
